cue: How do you say you'll do something quickly, on the fly?

es.meaning: Instantly, in mid-air — most often of catching an idea or a hint the moment it is offered.
es.example: No hizo falta explicárselo dos veces: lo cogió al vuelo.
es.exampleTranslation: Nobody had to explain it twice — she picked it up straight away.

it.literal: to do a thing at the flight
it.meaning: To do something quickly and without preparation — on the fly, in passing.
it.example: Passo al volo in farmacia e ti raggiungo.
it.exampleTranslation: I'll nip into the pharmacy and catch you up.

bridge.note: Identical words, identical image, and the target quietly narrows as you cross. Both languages picture something caught in mid-air before it lands. Italian lets you catch anything that way — an errand, a phone call, a task done in passing. Spanish aims almost entirely at one kind of object: an idea, a hint, an explanation. Coger algo al vuelo is about being quick on the uptake, not quick on your feet. The phrase survives the crossing; what it can be said about does not.

interference.es_to_it: Italian will take a far wider range of objects than Spanish habit suggests. 'Lo faccio al volo' about an errand, a repair, a quick trip — all natural in Italian, all outside the usual Spanish target.
interference.it_to_es: This is the direction that misfires. Say 'lo hago al vuelo' about fixing a shelf and a Spanish speaker hears something closer to 'I'll grasp it quickly' — a claim about comprehension, not about speed of work. For doing a task fast, Spanish reaches elsewhere: rápido, en un momento, de pasada.
